title: My aunt left me $6.4 million. The lawyer said I could keep it only if I confessed what I did at the county fair in 1987 (PART 2)

blocks.text: …I opened the sealed envelope that night, alone at my kitchen table. Inside was a newspaper clipping, a letter in Aunt Eleanor's shaky handwriting, and a photograph of me at sixteen with a bandage on my forehead, sitting on the back of an ambulance.
I didn't remember the ambulance. I didn't remember the bandage.

Eleanor's letter explained. On the last night of the fair in August 1987, a fire broke out in the hay barn next to the livestock pavilion during a crowded show. Hundreds of people rushed for the exits. The two main gates on that side were chained shut. The fair board's manager had ordered them locked that afternoon to stop teenagers from sneaking in without paying.
I was working the lemonade stand right beside one of those gates. I had seen the manager lock it.

And when people started screaming, I grabbed the bolt cutters from the maintenance shed, the ones I'd watched him use earlier, and cut the chain. Hundreds of people got out through that gate. Then I went back for the second one and was hit in the head by a falling beam. I woke up in the hospital two days later with a concussion and no memory of that night.
Forty-one people were injured, some badly. Nobody died, which the newspaper called a miracle.

The fair board's insurance company and its lawyers needed the story to be that the fire was an accident and the gates had been open. My aunt was the board's treasurer. She was offered a large payment to sign a statement saying the gates had never been locked. My parents, frightened of lawsuits and protective of me, agreed that I shouldn't be pressured to remember.
"You were a good child," Eleanor said in the video. "That's why we decided you shouldn't remember."
She took the money. She invested it for thirty-nine years and never spent a cent. It had grown to six point four million dollars. She couldn't bring herself to confess while she was alive.
"You're the only one left who knows why the gates were locked" wasn't quite true. I didn't know. But I could find out.

It took three months. I found the fair's former maintenance worker, now eighty-two, who confirmed he'd seen the manager lock the gates. I found the newspaper photographer, who still had negatives showing the cut chain. I found a woman who'd been a little girl that night and remembered a teenager in a lemonade apron with bolt cutters.
I made my statement at the county courthouse, in public, with the attorney beside me.

Then I handed the six point four million dollars to a settlement fund for the survivors and their families. Twenty-nine of the forty-one people injured were still alive. Most were in their sixties and seventies. Several had lived with burns and chronic pain for decades without compensation.
The fairgrounds put up a small plaque by the east gate last summer. It lists the names of everyone hurt that night. It doesn't mention me. I asked them not to.
But the woman who'd been a little girl that night found me afterward. She's in her forties now. She hugged me and said, "I always wondered what happened to the lemonade girl."
I still don't remember. I'm told that's all right.
